payload.say: Bible made with whole text in view; passage in front of drafter wins if it contradicts this. Open editor rulings pending on romanisation flavour (pinyin vs Japanese kundoku), on Master Sun vs Sun Sensei, and on capital-D Didacticism — interim defaults above preserve distance and strangeness. Do not resolve the worm; keep monk rude and motiveless, Liu neither fool nor victim, narrator visible but cool.
Drafted the opening tableau in a present-tense freeze, keeping heat, threshing ground, jar, and period terms stable.

payload.english: I

It is a heat such as has not been known in recent years. Whichever way you look, the roof-tiles of the mud-plastered houses throw back the sunlight dully, like lead, and even the swallows' nests hung beneath them, at this rate, look to steam their chicks and eggs to death where they lie. Still more, every field that is a field, whether hemp or millet, has bowed its head limply in the earth-steam, and not one thing keeps its green unwilted. The sky seen above those fields, perhaps stricken by the damp heat of these past days, is turbid and clouded near the ground though it is fine, and here and there the cloud-peaks float in drops, mere shapes, like hail parched in a roasting pan. — The tale of the "wine worm" begins with three men who have gone out of their way to come into a threshing ground in the blazing sun, in such weather.
notes: Kept the hail-parched-in-a-pan simile baldly as in the Japanese; it is meant to look forced and learned.

payload.english: Strangely, one of them lies stark naked, face upward on the bare ground. What is more, for some reason his hands and his feet are wound round and round with thin cord. Yet the man himself shows no particular sign of minding it. He is short, fresh-complexioned, somehow giving an impression of dull heaviness, a man fat as a pig. Then a handy unglazed jar stands at this man's pillow, but what may be inside that, too, is not known.

Another is a monk of strange and ancient visage at first sight, in a yellow robe with a small bronze ring hanging from his ear. His skin is black beyond the common, and to see his hair and beard all curled, he would seem a man come from somewhere west of the Onion Ranges. Until now he has patiently waved a fly-whisk with a red handle, driving from the naked man the horseflies and flies that would settle on him, but as might be expected looking a little tired, he has now come beside that same unglazed jar and squats there solemnly, in the posture of a turkey.
notes: Onion Ranges renders Sourrei in the text's own period geography for the Pamirs; fly-whisk renders shubi, the monk's horsehair whisk, in line without further gloss.

payload.english: The last one stands far apart from these two, under the eaves of a thatched hut in the corner of the threshing ground. This man grows on the tip of his chin a merely formal beard like a rat's tail, and his rig is a soap-black cloth gown long enough to hide his heels, with a tea-brown sash whose knot hangs slovenly down. Judging by the way he now and then uses with care a fan made of white bird feathers, he is most likely a Confucian scholar or something of the sort.

These three men, all three as if by agreement, hold their tongues. Moreover they scarcely so much as stir, so that you would think they take an extraordinary interest in something about to happen, and for that are all holding their breath.

The sun must be exactly at midday. Perhaps because even the dogs are napping, not a single bark is heard. The hemp and millet hemming the threshing ground gloss their green leaves in the sun and rest hushed and utterly still. And then the sky seen beyond them drifts everywhere oppressively with shimmering haze, so that you suspect even the cloud-peaks are panting in this drought. As far as the eye reaches, nothing seems to breathe but these three men. And those three, again, keep their silence like the clay images enshrined in a Lord Guan temple....
Of course, this is no tale of Japan. — It is an event that happened one summer on the threshing ground of the Liu family at a place called Chozan in China.

payload.say: Drafted section two exposition and interview in dry antiquarian voice, keeping monk blunt and narrator digressive.

payload.english: II

The man lying naked in the blazing sun is the master of this threshing ground, a man surnamed Liu and named Dacheng, one of the foremost rich men of Chozan. This man's pleasure is drink and drink alone; from morning on he is scarcely ever known to part from his cup. And that, as the phrase has it, "whenever he drank alone, he would at once empty a whole jar" — a capacity beyond the common run of men. Though, as I have said before, "his fields by the city wall number three hundred mu, half sown with millet," so there was not the least fear that drink should encumber his estate.
notes: Kanbun-style tags kept as quoted lore; jar and mu kept stable per bible. No gloss added.

payload.english: Why he should be lying naked in the blazing sun has a history of this sort. — That day, as Liu sat together with his fellow-drinker Sun Sensei, Master Sun (the Confucian scholar with the white-feather fan), in a well-aired room, leaning on his bamboo wife and fighting out a match on the board, a maidservant came in to say, "A monk lodging, so he says, at Hodoji or somewhere, has come and insists on seeing you, master — how shall I answer him?"
notes: First mention glosses Sensei as Master Sun per bible; bamboo wife left to context; Hodoji kept as temple name.

payload.english: "What, Hodoji?" So saying, Liu blinked his small eyes as if dazzled, then, raising his fat body that looked hot already, ordered, "Show him in here." Then, with a glance at Sun Sensei's face, he added, "It must be that monk, I suppose."

The monk at Hodoji is a barbarian monk come from the Western Regions. Since he both practises medicine and administers arts of the bedchamber, his fame stands high in this neighbourhood — that Chang San's black cataract suddenly took a turn for the better, for instance, or that Li Si's impotence was healed on the spot — rumours all but miraculous are rife. — Both men had heard these rumours. What business could that barbarian monk now have, to go out of his way to visit Liu? Of course, Liu had no recollection whatever of having sent for him.
notes: barbarian monk kept as period reportage; Zhang San / Li Si as generic hearsay names.

payload.english: Let me say in passing that Liu is not by nature a man who welcomes visitors. But when one guest is already present and a new guest arrives, he will generally receive him gladly. For he has a childish vanity that might be described as showing off, before his guest, that he has guests. Moreover this barbarian monk of today is the talk of every quarter of late. By no means a guest to be ashamed of meeting. — Liu's motives in offering to meet him lay roughly here.
notes: Narrator's digression on vanity kept as aside, not smoothed to transition.

payload.english: "What can be his business?"
"Alms-begging, most likely. Asking us to bestow alms, I suppose."
notes: No dialogue tags added; speakers left to inference as in Japanese.

payload.english: While the two were talking thus, presently, led in by the maidservant, there appeared a misshapen monk of tall stature, with eyes like purple quartz. In a yellow robe, his grown-out curling hair hanging troublesomely over his shoulders, he stood heavily in the middle of the room with his red-handled fly-whisk still in hand. No greeting, not a word.
notes: fly-whisk kept stable; strangeness reported plainly without intensifying.

payload.english: Liu hesitated for a while, but as it somehow grew unsettling, he ventured, "Have you some business with us?"
Then the barbarian monk said, "You, I take it, are fond of wine."
notes: Monk's bluntness kept short; no softening.

payload.english: "Indeed." Liu, the question being so abrupt, answered vaguely, looking toward Sun Sensei as if seeking rescue. Sun Sensei, composed, was laying stones on the board by himself. He showed no disposition to take part.
"You suffer from a rare disease. Did you know it?" The barbarian monk said this as if to press the point. Liu, hearing of disease, wore a dubious look, stroking his bamboo wife as
"A disease — you say?"
"Just so."
"Why, from my childhood —" As Liu would say something, the barbarian monk cut him off,
"Drink as you will, you never get drunk, do you?"
"..." Liu stared at his interlocutor and shut his mouth. In fact, drink as this man would, he had never once been drunk.

"That is the proof of the disease." The barbarian monk, with a thin smile, went on, "A wine worm lives in your belly. Unless it is removed, this disease will not heal. I, this poor monk, have come to heal your disease."
notes: wine worm kept lower-case and stable; poor monk for humble priestly I.

payload.english: "Can it be healed?" Liu uttered, involuntarily, in an uncertain voice. And was himself ashamed of it.
"Healed — that is why I came."
Then Sun Sensei, who had till now listened in silence to the exchange, suddenly put in a word.
"Do you employ some medicine?"
"No, there is no need to employ medicine or the like." The barbarian monk answered ungraciously.

Sun Sensei from the first all but unreasoningly despises the two teachings of Dao and Buddha. Hence he very rarely speaks when thrown together with a Daoist priest or a monk. That he should now suddenly feel moved to speak was wholly because the word wine worm had caught his interest, for the wine-loving Sensei, on hearing it, grew a little uneasy lest a wine worm dwell in his own belly too. Hearing, however, the barbarian monk's reluctant answer, he suddenly felt as if he had been made a fool of, so with a slight frown the Sensei fell again as before to laying out his pieces in silence. And at the same time he recalled within himself that his host Liu, who would meet such an arrogant monk, was absurd.
notes: Sensei's self-interested anxiety and contempt kept flat; monk neither villain nor saint.

payload.english: Liu, for his part, of course paid no heed to any such thing.
"Then do you use needles?"
"Nothing so elaborate as that."
"Then is it an incantation?"
"No, nor is it an incantation."

After repeating such exchanges, the barbarian monk briefly explained his cure to them. — According to it, one need only strip naked and lie still in the sun. To Liu it seemed a very easy matter. If so small a thing would heal him, there was nothing better than to be healed. Moreover, though he was not conscious of it, curiosity was also somewhat stirred at the prospect of undergoing the barbarian monk's treatment.
notes: Liu's consent kept as vanity and curiosity, not suffering.

payload.english: So that at last Liu himself bowed his head and it was agreed: "Then pray heal me, if you will." — Such is the history behind Liu's lying naked on the threshing ground in the blazing sun.

The barbarian monk then, saying he must not stir, wound Liu's body round and round with thin cord. Then he bade one of the manservants bring a single wine-filled unglazed jar to Liu's pillow. That Sun Sensei, his good friend on the wine-mound, should by the turn of the moment stand witness to this strange cure goes without saying.
notes: good friend on the wine-mound kept as mock-heroic tag; the jar kept stable.

payload.english: What sort of thing a wine worm is, what becomes of one when it is gone from the belly, what the wine jar at the pillow is meant for — none knows these things but the barbarian monk. Put so, Liu, who has gone out naked into the blazing sun knowing nothing, may seem exceedingly improvident, but what ordinary men undergo when they receive a school education, for instance, is in truth for the most part the doing of the same sort of thing.
notes: Sly dig at Liu and at schooling preserved as narrator's aside.

payload.say: Drafted the ordeal in long cumulative sentences with present-tense bodily sensation preserved.

payload.english: III

It is hot. Sweat wells prickling up on his forehead, and when it seems to have beaded it comes trickling lukewarm toward his eyes. As ill luck will have it he is bound with thin cord, so of course he cannot put out a hand to wipe it away. He tries moving his neck to turn the sweat from its path, but at that instant he feels a violent dizziness about to come on, so to his regret he gives up that plan too. Meanwhile the sweat unreservedly wets his eyelids, and circling from the side of his nose round his mouth, runs down under his chin. The nastiness is beyond measure.
notes: Kept the opening present tense and the long cumulative sweat sentences long; the short close is kept short and flat.

payload.english: Until then he had kept his eyes open, gazing hard at the sky scorched white and the hemp-field with its drooping leaves, but once the sweat began to pour without restraint he had to give even that up. It was then that Liu learned for the first time that sweat stings when it gets into the eyes. So, wearing the face of a sheep in the slaughterhouse, meekly shutting his eyes while he lies still beneath the beating sun, he begins by degrees to feel a certain pain in the skin of the upper parts of him, face or body alike. Over the whole surface of the skin a force is at work urging it to move in every direction at once, while the skin itself has not the least elasticity to answer it with; a pain that might best be described as a smarting everywhere. This is not the misery of mere sweating. Liu began to feel a little bitter at having taken the barbarian monk's cure.
notes: 汗所 rendered as 'mere sweating' — literal sense uncertain, left flat rather than medicalized.
Narrator's 'to Betsu suru' hedge kept as 'might best be described as'.

payload.english: Yet this, as he came to think afterward, was still of the less painful order. — Before long his throat grew parched. Liu too knows the tale of how Cao Mengde, or someone, doctored his soldiers' thirst by telling them there was a plum grove ahead. But in this present case, however he pictures the sweet-sour plum in his mind, his throat is thirsty just the same as before. He moves his chin, he bites his tongue, but the inside of his mouth still holds its heat. Even that might have been a little easier to bear, had it not been for the unglazed jar at his pillow. For from the mouth of the jar the rich fumes of wine assail his nose without pause. And, perhaps only in fancy, that reek seems to grow stronger with every minute. Thinking at least to look at the jar, Liu opens his eyes. Straining them upward, he takes in the mouth of the jar and perhaps half of its generously swollen belly. That is all he takes in with his eyes, but at the same time there rises in his imagination the golden-yellow wine lying brimful and still in the jar's dim interior. Before he knows it he licks his cracked lips round with his dry tongue, but there is no sign of saliva welling. Even his sweat by now is dried by the sun and no longer flows as before.
notes: Cao Mengde allusion glossed in line only, as 'telling them there was a plum grove ahead', without further history.
上眼 rendered as straining the eyes upward from a bound, supine position.

payload.english: Then violent dizziness comes, two or three times in succession. The headache has been unbroken since a while back. In his heart Liu curses the barbarian monk ever more bitterly. And then he thinks too why a man such as himself should have ridden on such a fellow's cajolery into this idiotic suffering. Meanwhile his throat grows ever thirstier. His chest turns strangely queasy. He can no longer lie still for endurance. So at last, resolving himself, Liu opens his gasping mouth, meaning to beg the monk at his pillow to stop the cure. —

But at that very instant. Liu begins to feel an unnameable lump creeping little by little up from his breast toward his throat. At one moment it seems to writhe like an earthworm, at another to edge itself along like a gecko. In any case some soft thing, soft as it is, comes squirming up the gullet. And at last, when it seems to have forced its way beneath his Adam's apple, all at once it slips like a loach or something out of the dark and flies outwards with force.
notes: Kept the odd simile sequence earthworm-gecko-loach in order, without unifying or prettifying.

payload.english: At that moment, from the quarter of that same unglazed jar, comes a small plop, as of something dropping into wine.
At this the monk abruptly lifts the haunches he had settled and begins to undo the thin cord wound about Liu's body. The wine worm is out now, he says, he may rest easy.

"Is it out?" Liu says this as if groaning, and raising his reeling head, out of curiosity forgets even his thirst and crawls naked to the side of the jar. Seeing it, Sun Sensei too, shading the sun with his white-feather fan, hurries toward the two. When all three peer together into the jar, there is a small thing like a salamander, its flesh the colour of red clay, swimming in the wine. It must be about three sun in length. It has a mouth, it has eyes. Somehow it seems to drink as it swims. Seeing this, Liu suddenly feels sick. ...
notes: 'Three sun' kept as period measure, about nine centimetres, left to context.
Worm kept as 'thing like a salamander' with mouth and eyes; not ennobled to spirit or demon.

payload.say: Drafted the aftermath and three-answer close, keeping cure and ruin complete and the refusal flat.

payload.english: IV

The barbarian monk's cure showed its effect on the spot. From that day Liu Dacheng quite suddenly could drink no more. Now, he says, he cannot even bear the smell. Yet strangely, his health from that time began to fail little by little. This year is the third since he spat out the wine worm, and no trace remains of the round and sleek fullness of former years. Skin of a poor lustre hangs greasily over the bones of a gaunt face, and only a little hair, touched with frost, lingers upon his temples; they say there is no telling how many times in a year he takes to his bed.
notes: Kept the paired body terms plain: frost-touched hair upon the temples, dull greasy skin over bone, to hold the counter-repetition to his former fatness.

payload.english: But it is not his health alone that has declined since then. His fortune too has gone steadily downhill, and now of the suburban fields counted at three hundred mu, most have passed into other hands. Liu himself has willy-nilly taken hoe in unpractised hands, and passes his wretched day-to-day existence.

Why, since spitting out the wine worm, has Liu's health failed? Why has his fortune declined — once the spitting of the worm and Liu's later ruin are set side by side as cause and effect, these are questions anyone is likely to ask. In fact this question has been repeated by people of every trade living in Chozan, and answered from the mouths of those same people in every kind of way. The three answers given here are in truth no more than the most representative chosen from among them.
First answer. The wine worm was Liu's fortune, and not Liu's sickness. By chancing upon a benighted barbarian monk, he willingly brought about the loss of this heaven-sent fortune.

Second answer. The wine worm was Liu's sickness, and not Liu's fortune. For to drain a whole jar at a single drinking is quite beyond what an ordinary man can conceive. Had the worm not been removed, Liu must before long have died, without question. Seen in this light, poverty and sickness coming by turns should rather be called happiness for Liu.

Third answer. The wine worm was neither Liu's sickness nor Liu's fortune. Liu from of old did nothing but drink. If wine were taken from Liu's life, nothing would remain behind. Thus Liu is the wine worm, the wine worm is Liu. Therefore Liu's parting with the wine worm was the same as killing himself. In short, from the day he could drink no more, Liu was Liu and yet not Liu. If Liu himself had already ceased to be, then it is entirely natural that the health and fortune of the Liu of former days should have been lost.
notes: Kept the identity bald — Liu is the wine worm, the wine worm is Liu — and the paradox Liu was Liu and yet not Liu, without softening into metaphor, as the crux requires.

payload.english: Which of these answers best hits the mark, I myself do not know. I have merely, in imitation of the Didacticism of the Chinese novelists, set down such moral judgments in a list at the end of this tale.
notes: Kept the alien capital D in Didacticism as in the source.

payload.english: — April of the Fifth Year —
notes: Date left as written; understood as the first-publication date.

hard_spots.why_hard: Two unglossed Chinese tags define Liu's excess and immunity from ruin: 独酌する毎に輒一甕を尽す (drinks a whole jar at a sitting) and 負郭の田三百畝半は黍を種う (300 mu of suburban fields, half in millet). Syntax is Sino-Japanese kundoku; English must render as quoted lore without explanatory footnote, keeping jar and mu stable.

Cao Mengde's 前路に梅林あり ruse (quenching thirst by talking of plums) is assumed known. Liu tries it and fails. English needs in-text light touch so reader gets the point — talk cannot quench real thirst — without a lecture on Three Kingdoms history.

Extraction similes come in odd deliberate sequence: earthworm-like peristalsis, gecko-like clinging, loach-like slippery dash; then the worm itself like a tiny red-clay-coloured salamander (山椒魚) three sun long, with mouth and eyes, apparently drinking as it swims. Keep sequence and disgust; do not prettify into spirit/demon or unify into one animal. Period body terms with ruby (眶, 喉仏, 双髩, 顳顬) add learned texture.

hard_spots.kind: philosophical equation plus alien English loan
hard_spots.why_hard: Third answer's bald identity 劉即酒虫酒虫即劉 (Liu is the worm, the worm is Liu) must stay bald and logical, not softened to metaphor (part of him). Final paragraph's capitalised English Didacticism stands out in Japanese; keeping the capital preserves ironic distance from the device being used. Both are the crux's load-bearing points.

Text estranges its own readers with rubied Sino-Japanese: 打麦場, 燕, 霰を炮烙で煎つたやうな雲, 竹婦人, 白羽扇, 皁布衫, 茶褐帯, 麈尾, 法衣, 青銅の環, 関帝廟泥塑像. English must keep a small stable set with once-only light gloss in line; footnoting every object fails the keikaku test, domesticating all flattens the vernacular layering which here IS the exotic register.

蛮僧, 西域, 葱嶺の西, skin black, curly hair/beard, bronze earring, purple-stone eyes. Must report period vocabulary plainly (barbarian monk from the Western Regions) without modernising away or leaning into caricature; monk must stay rude and motiveless, neither villain nor saint.

motifs.english: Translate invariably as 'wine worm' (singular, lower case); never spirit, demon, parasite, bug. Keep indefinite at first, definite after expulsion.
motifs.why: Title-thing and undecided equation: disease, fortune, or Liu himself. Varying the word decides what the tale withholds; stability lets the three final answers bite the same object.

motifs.english: Keep invariably 'the unglazed jar' / 'the jar'; wine fragrance rising from it strengthens by the minute in ordeal.
motifs.motif: the unglazed earthenware jar of wine at the pillow
motifs.why: Bait-trap and measure: mysterious at tableau, lure in thirst, plop-marks expulsion, tank where worm swims drinking. Must stay same homely object, not ennobled to urn or vessel.

motifs.english: Keep heat lexis blunt and cumulative: blazing sun, scorching noon, leaden tiles, steaming air. Do not vary into synonyms for elegance.
motifs.why: Opens with leaden tiles, steaming swallow's nest, wilting hemp/millet, turbid air; ordeal replays it on skin, sweat, thirst. After cure, counter-repetition is decline. Breaking the chain loses the tale's weather-body.

motifs.english: Keep fatness lexis stable: fat like a pig, round and sleek; then counter-lexis: skin loose on bone, frost-touched temples. Do not euphemise.
motifs.motif: fatness then wasting; fields then loss
motifs.why: Body and fortune mirror the undecided cure: complete success (cannot even stand the smell) and complete uselessness (health and 300 mu waste away). Prettifying or moralising either side tips the ending.

narration.english_tense: Past as default for backstory and aftermath, but preserve present-tense freeze for the opening tableau (pp2-8) and for immediate bodily sensation in the ordeal (sweat, prickling, thirst in pp44-48); do not normalise all to past or chop long cumulative sentences into brisk beats, nor join short declaratives elsewhere.
narration.frame: Four numbered movements: 1 tableau held in silence, 2 exposition and interview (why Liu meets the monk), 3 ordeal in the body, 4 aftermath and three-answer moral list with flat refusal. Narrator intrudes to locate tale (of course not Japan but Chozan China), apologise for digressions, explain Liu's childish vanity, and compare blind submission to the cure with ordinary schooling.
narration.narrator: Learned-amateur reteller of a Chinese strange tale: amused, scholarly, slightly superior, never intimate; digressive on purpose (as I said before, let me add in passing); allows one sly dig at Liu and at schooling (p42) but otherwise withholds judgment to earn the final I-don't-know.
narration.person: Third person throughout with first-person intrusions (自分 in p59, and metanarrative asides); not a character in the action
narration.tense_habits: Taisho literary mixed -ru present tableau and -ta past anecdote; opens in vivid present (である, してゐる), backstory in past, ordeal slides between gnomic present (暑い) and past perception (知った), aftermath in summary past with present result (飲めなくなった, 衰へて来た)
timeline: Unnamed summer noon: Liu bound naked on his threshing ground, ordeal and expulsion same afternoon
Three years after spitting the worm to present of telling: progressive wasting of body and estate
Coda dated 五年四月 (April of year 5 — Taisho 5 / 1916, first-publication date): narrator lists three morals and declines choice

bible.say: Bible made with whole text in view; passage in front of drafter wins if it contradicts this. Open editor rulings pending on romanisation flavour (pinyin vs Japanese kundoku), on Master Sun vs Sun Sensei, and on capital-D Didacticism — interim defaults above preserve distance and strangeness. Do not resolve the worm; keep monk rude and motiveless, Liu neither fool nor victim, narrator visible but cool.

style_sheet.annotation_density: Minimal; keikaku test applies with force to a story already wearing erudition. Gloss bamboo wife, fly-whisk, mu, jar in line once or leave to context; no footnotes for every object. Only terms a reader cannot recover from context get a note.
style_sheet.author_voice: Akutagawa grafting modern physiological interiority onto an old anecdote: learned Sino-Japanese surface with furigana, precise similes in odd sequence, flat affect against disgust, ending in performed-and-mocked Chinese moralising. English: measured slightly formal prose, long cumulative sentences in ordeal kept long, short declaratives elsewhere kept short; no elegance creep.
style_sheet.honorifics_and_names: Surname-first for Chinese names pending editor ruling (interim pinyin: Liu Dacheng, Zhang San, Li Si, Cao Mengde; Japanese kundoku reading recorded in cast). Keep Sensei in Sun Sensei on first mention with light gloss Master Sun to signal Confucian status; thereafter Sun Sensei invariably. Keep Sensei even where English would reach for a name — the relation is in the title. Monk has no name; keep barbarian monk as period reportage.
style_sheet.keep_in_japanese: Translate most objects (threshing ground, unglazed jar, white-feather fan, bamboo wife) with once-only light gloss; retain in italics only a handful where English has no equivalent and strangeness is wanted: e.g. 竹婦人 bamboo wife, 麈尾 fly-whisk, 畝 mu. Never footnote ordinary usage.
style_sheet.quotation: Japanese 「」 and 『』 to English double quotes; monk's bluntness kept in short sentences; interior sensation left without quotes. No added dialogue tags where Japanese leaves speaker to inference.
style_sheet.register: Measured, slightly formal narrative English for a Taisho learned tale; dialogue plain and blunt, not colloquial-modern. Keep faintly exotic surface; do not domesticate into Anglo-Saxon plainness nor ennoble into high style.
style_sheet.ruby_and_italics: Ruby in source signals learned showing-off; render with italics on first use of retained terms only, with in-line gloss (bamboo wife, fly-whisk). Keep alien capital D in Didacticism. Do not italicise wine worm, threshing ground, the jar — they are stable English motifs, not foreign words.

このファイルは、インターネットの図書館、青空文庫（http://www.aozora.gr.jp/）で作られました。入力、校正、制作にあたったのは、ボランティアの皆さんです。

crux.for_the_english: Keep the cure's success complete and useless: he really cannot drink afterward, and he really wastes away; let both stand without reconciling them. Preserve the narrator's flat “I don't know” and the slightly parodic list of morals at the end — any translation that nudges toward the third answer, the most elegant one, or that colours the monk as villain or saviour, has decided what the text leaves open. Keep the monk rude, abrupt, and motiveless; keep Liu neither fool nor victim, though the narrator allows a brief sly dig at him (and at ordinary people submitting to schooling) along the way.
crux.point: The cure works, and the cure is the ruin — and the narrator refuses to say what the worm was. Was it Liu's disease, his fortune, or simply Liu himself, so that expelling it emptied the man? The story ends by formally listing all three answers and declining to choose, in open imitation of a Chinese tale's didactic close. Everything in the telling is built to earn that refusal: the monk arrives uninvited and unexplained, diagnoses without evidence, cures without medicine, and vanishes from the story without reward or comment; Liu consents out of vanity and curiosity more than suffering, since his 'disease' has never once made him drunk or cost him anything.
crux.why: Because the tale has almost no plot beyond extraction-and-decline, its meaning lives entirely in that undecided equation. If the English tips the balance — making the worm a blessing foolishly lost, or a parasite rightly removed at a sad price — it becomes a fable with a moral, which is exactly the kind of Chinese-novel Didacticism the last paragraph is both performing and mocking.

open_questions.question: How far to signal the Chinese source-text flavour in names and terms — Wade-Giles-flavoured or modern pinyin renderings, retained terms with a light gloss, or plain English equivalents? The Japanese text estranges its own readers with rubied Sino-Japanese terms; some equivalent distance is wanted, but the system needs an editor's ruling before drafting.
open_questions.why_it_matters: Too much apparatus turns a swift tale into a museum piece; too little makes the setting generic.

open_questions.question: Should the final 'Didacticism' stay capitalised and slightly alien in English, as it stands out in the Japanese, or be naturalised to 'moralising'? Keeping the capital preserves the narrator's ironic distance from the device he is using; naturalising smooths it away.

How blunt should the monk's speech be? He is peremptory to the edge of rudeness in Japanese, and Sun's offence at it matters; but overdone curtness in English could make him a stage 'inscrutable Oriental' villain, which the text does not support.

The third answer's equation — Liu is the wine worm, the wine worm is Liu — should it be kept in that bald, almost Buddhist logical form, or softened into metaphor ('the worm was part of him')? The reading above requires the bald form, but the editor may want the fork recorded.

reading.reading:
The crux comes first above; what follows is how it plays through the telling. The story is a retold Chinese strange tale, and it knows it: the narrator opens not in China but on a frozen noon tableau — a naked man bound hand and foot in a threshing ground, a dark foreign monk fanning flies from him, a Confucian scholar pointedly apart under the eaves — and only after holding that silence does he step in to say, of course, this is not Japan, but Chōzan in China, at the Liu family's threshing ground. Keep that order and that intrusion. The narrator throughout is a learned amateur telling an anecdote: he says 'as I mentioned before,' apologises for a digression about why Liu agreed to meet the monk, explains Liu's childish vanity about having a guest to show off, and at one point compares submitting blindly to the monk's cure with ordinary people submitting to school education. Those asides are not decoration to be trimmed; they set the temperature — amused, scholarly, slightly superior, never intimate — against which the ending's refusal to judge can register. A fluent draft will be tempted to make the narrator invisible and let the tale 'speak for itself.' Resist that.

Register is Taishō literary Japanese saturated with Sino-Japanese vocabulary that the original itself glosses with furigana — threshing ground, bamboo wife, white-feather fan, the monk's fly-whisk, Liu's fields measured in hundreds of mu. That learned, faintly exotic surface is the tale's China: a literary place, not a reported one. In English, keep a measured, slightly formal narrative prose and let a small number of retained terms carry the foreignness, glossed once and lightly or left to context; do not footnote every object (the house's keikaku test applies with special force to a story already wearing its erudition on its sleeve), and do not domesticate everything into plain Anglo-Saxon either, which would flatten the vernacular layering Berman warns about — here, the exotic register is the vernacular. Names and the monk's speech need care: he is a 'barbarian monk' from the Western Regions in the text's own period vocabulary, dark-skinned, curly-haired, with a bronze ear-ring, and the English should report that period gaze plainly rather than either modernising it away or leaning into it.

The shape is four numbered movements: tableau, exposition and interview, ordeal, aftermath. The middle of the piece, and its most modern passage, is the ordeal in section three, where the narration drops into Liu's bound body — sweat running into his eyes and teaching him for the first time that sweat stings, skin prickling as if pulled in all directions at once, thirst sharpened by the smell of wine from the jar at his pillow, then the thing crawling up his gullet, now like an earthworm, now like a gecko, now slipping out like a loach. This is Akutagawa grafting physiological interiority onto an old anecdote, and it must stay visceral and a little disgusting, its similes kept in their odd sequence rather than varied or prettified. The sentences here run long and cumulative; do not chop them into brisk modern beats, and equally do not join the short declarative sentences elsewhere into graceful compounds. Heat is the binding repetition: the leaden roof tiles, the steaming swallow's nest, the wilting hemp and millet, the three men silent as clay temple statues — and after the cure, the counter-repetition of decline, fat gone, skin loose on bone, fields passing to other hands. Keep 'wine worm,' 'threshing ground,' 'the jar,' and Liu's fatness verbally stable so that network survives; ennobling the worm into a 'spirit' or 'demon,' or explaining what it 'really' is, would be clarification of exactly what the tale withholds — nobody in the story, the narrator included, ever says.

Likely fluent failures, in order of danger: moralising the ending; making the monk sinister or saintly; smoothing the narrator's digressions into transitions; prettifying the ordeal; over-explaining Chinese terms; and warming Liu into a lovable drunk, which would pre-decide the third answer emotionally before the reader reaches it.
reading.say: The crux is that the cure works and ruins him, and the narrator lists three morals — disease, fortune, or the man himself — and refuses to choose; keep the monk motiveless, the narrator's digressive antiquarian voice intact, and the bound body's ordeal as visceral as it is, so the ending's refusal lands.

voice_takes.label: Dry antiquarian
voice_takes.line: Cool, formal, deadpan storyteller, letting the digressions and the final refusal carry the irony — the reading's first choice.

voice_takes.label: Plainer and more physical
voice_takes.line: Less learned surface, harder emphasis on heat, sweat, and thirst; risks thinning the Chinese-tale flavour.

voice_takes.label: Warmer fabulist
voice_takes.line: A rounder, more oral tale-telling warmth; risks nudging Liu toward the lovable drunk and pre-deciding the moral.

casual.en: I

casual.en: It is a heat such as has not been known in recent years. Whichever way you look, the roof-tiles of the mud-plastered houses throw back the sunlight dully, like lead, and even the swallows' nests hung beneath them, at this rate, look to steam their chicks and eggs to death where they lie. Still more, every field that is a field, whether hemp or millet, has bowed its head limply in the earth-steam, and not one thing keeps its green unwilted. The sky seen above those fields, perhaps stricken by the damp heat of these past days, is turbid and clouded near the ground though it is fine, and here and there the cloud-peaks float in drops, mere shapes, like hail parched in a roasting pan. — The tale of the "wine worm" begins with three men who have gone out of their way to come into a threshing ground in the blazing sun, in such weather.
casual.ja: 近年にない暑さである。どこを見ても、泥で固めた家々の屋根瓦が、鉛のやうに鈍く日の光を反射して、その下に懸けてある燕の巣さへ、この塩梅では中にゐる雛や卵を、そのまゝ蒸殺してしまふかと思はれる。まして、畑と云ふ畑は、麻でも黍でも、皆、土いきれにぐつたりと頭をさげて、何一つ、青いなりに、萎れてゐないものはない。その畑の上に見える空も、この頃の温気に中てられたせいか、地上に近い大気は、晴れながら、どんよりと濁つて、その所々に、霰を炮烙で煎つたやうな、形ばかりの雲の峰が、つぶつぶと浮かんでゐる。――「酒虫」の話は、この陽気に、わざ〳〵炎天の打麦場へ出てゐる、三人の男で始まるのである。
casual.label: house-checked

casual.en: Strangely, one of them lies stark naked, face upward on the bare ground. What is more, for some reason his hands and his feet are wound round and round with thin cord. Yet the man himself shows no particular sign of minding it. He is short, fresh-complexioned, somehow giving an impression of dull heaviness, a man fat as a pig. Then a handy unglazed jar stands at this man's pillow, but what may be inside that, too, is not known.
casual.ja: 不思議な事に、その中の一人は、素裸で、仰向けに地面へ寝ころんでゐる。おまけに、どう云ふ訳だか、細引で、手も足もぐる〳〵巻にされてゐる。が格別当人は、それを苦に病んでゐる容子もない。背の低い、血色の好い、どことなく鈍重と云ふ感じを起させる、豚のやうに肥つた男である。それから手ごろな素焼の瓶が一つ、この男の枕もとに置いてあるが、これも中に何がはいつてゐるのだか、わからない。
casual.label: house-checked

casual.en: Another is a monk of strange and ancient visage at first sight, in a yellow robe with a small bronze ring hanging from his ear. His skin is black beyond the common, and to see his hair and beard all curled, he would seem a man come from somewhere west of the Onion Ranges. Until now he has patiently waved a fly-whisk with a red handle, driving from the naked man the horseflies and flies that would settle on him, but as might be expected looking a little tired, he has now come beside that same unglazed jar and squats there with ponderous self-importance, in the posture of a turkey.
casual.ja: もう一人は、黄色い法衣を着て、耳に小さな青銅の環をさげた、一見、象貌の奇古な沙門である。皮膚の色が並はづれて黒い上に、髪や鬚の縮れてゐる所を見ると、どうも葱嶺の西からでも来た人間らしい。これはさつきから根気よく、朱柄の麈尾をふりふり、裸の男にたからうとする虻や蠅を追つてゐたが、流石に少しくたびれたと見えて、今では、例の素焼の瓶の側へ来て、七面鳥のやうな恰好をしながら、勿体らしくしやがんでゐる。
casual.label: house-checked

casual.en: The last one stands far apart from these two, under the eaves of a thatched hut in the corner of the threshing ground. This man grows on the tip of his chin a merely formal beard like a rat's tail, and he is dressed in a soap-black cloth gown long enough to hide his heels, with a tea-brown sash whose knot hangs slovenly down. Judging by the way he now and then uses with care a fan made of white bird feathers, he is most likely a Confucian scholar or something of the sort.
casual.ja: あとの一人は、この二人からずつと離れて、打麦場の隅にある草房の軒下に立つてゐる。この男は、頤の先に、鼠の尻尾のやうな髯を、申訳だけに生やして、踵が隠れる程長い皁布衫に、結目をだらしなく垂らした茶褐帯と云ふ拵へである。白い鳥の羽で製つた団扇を、時々大事さうに使つてゐる容子では、多分、儒者か何かにちがひない。
casual.label: house-checked

casual.en: These three men, all three as if by agreement, hold their tongues. Moreover they scarcely so much as stir, so that you would think they take an extraordinary interest in something about to happen, and for that are all holding their breath.
casual.ja: この三人が三人とも、云ひ合せたやうに、口を噤んでゐる。その上、碌に身動きさへもしない、何か、これから起らうとする事に、非常な興味でも持つてゐて、その為に、皆、息をひそめてゐるのではないかと思はれる。
casual.label: house-checked

casual.en: The sun must be exactly at midday. Perhaps because even the dogs are napping, not a single bark is heard. The hemp and millet hemming the threshing ground gloss their green leaves in the sun and rest hushed and utterly still. And then the sky seen beyond them drifts everywhere oppressively with shimmering haze, so that you suspect even the cloud-peaks are panting in this drought. As far as the eye reaches, nothing seems to breathe but these three men. And those three, again, keep their silence like the clay images enshrined in a Lord Guan temple....
casual.ja: 日は正に、亭午であらう。犬も午睡をしてゐるせいか、吠える声一つ聞えない。打麦場を囲んでゐる麻や黍も、青い葉を日に光らせて、ひつそりかんと静まつてゐる。それから、その末に見える空も、一面に、熱くるしく、炎靄をたゞよはせて、雲の峰さへもこの旱に、肩息をついてゐるのかと、疑はれる。見渡した所、息が通つてゐるらしいのは、この三人の男の外にない。さうして、その三人が又、関帝廟に安置してある、泥塑の像のやうに沈黙を守つてゐる。……
casual.label: house-checked

casual.en: Of course, this is no tale of Japan. — It is an event that happened one summer on the threshing ground of the Liu family at a place called Chozan in China.
casual.ja: 勿論、日本の話ではない。――支那の長山と云ふ所にある劉氏の打麦場で、或年の夏、起つた出来事である。
casual.label: house-checked

casual.en: II
casual.ja: 二
casual.label: house-checked

casual.en: The man lying naked in the blazing sun is the master of this threshing ground, a man surnamed Liu and named Dacheng, one of the foremost rich men of Chozan. This man's pleasure is drink and drink alone; from morning on he is scarcely ever known to part from his cup. And that, as the phrase has it, "whenever he drank alone, he would at once empty a whole jar" — a capacity beyond the common run of men. Though, as I have said before, "his fields by the city wall number three hundred mu, half sown with millet," so there was not the least fear that drink should encumber his estate.
casual.ja: 裸で、炎天に寝ころんでゐるのは、この打麦場の主人で、姓は劉、名は大成と云ふ、長山では、屈指の素封家の一人である。この男の道楽は、酒を飲む一方で、朝から、殆、盃を離したと云ふ事がない。それも、「独酌する毎に輒、一甕を尽す」と云ふのだから、人並をはづれた酒量である。尤も前にも云つたやうに、「負郭の田三百畝、半は黍を種う」と云ふので、飲の為に家産が累はされるやうな惧は、万々ない。
casual.label: house-checked

notes.body: A mu is a traditional Chinese unit of field area; three hundred mu marks Liu as a very large landowner.

casual.en: Why he should be lying naked in the blazing sun has a history of this sort. — That day, as Liu sat together with his fellow-drinker Sun Sensei, Master Sun (the Confucian scholar with the white-feather fan), in a well-aired room, leaning on his bamboo wife and fighting out a match on the board, a maidservant came in to say, "A monk lodging, so he says, at Hodoji or somewhere, has come and insists on seeing you, master — how shall I answer him?"
casual.ja: それが、何故、裸で、炎天に寝ころんでゐるかと云ふと、それには、かう云ふ因縁がある。――その日、劉が、同じ飲仲間の孫先生と一しよに（これが、白羽扇を持つてゐた儒者である。）風通しのいゝ室で、竹婦人に靠れながら、棋局を闘はせてゐると、召使ひの丫鬟が来て、「唯今、宝幢寺とかにゐると云ふ、坊さんが御見えになりまして、是非、御主人に御目にかゝりたいと申しますが、いかゞ致しませう。」と云ふ。
casual.label: house-checked

notes.body: A hollow bolster woven from bamboo, leaned against in summer to keep cool while reclining.

casual.en: "What, Hodoji?" So saying, Liu blinked his small eyes as if dazzled, then, raising his fat body that looked hot already, ordered, "Show him in here." Then, with a glance at Sun Sensei's face, he added, "It must be that monk, I suppose."
casual.ja: 「なに、宝幢寺？」かう云つて、劉は小さな眼を、まぶしさうに、しばたたいたが、やがて、暑さうに肥つた体を起しながら、「では、こゝへ御通し申せ。」と云ひつけた。それから、孫先生の顔をちよいと見て「大方あの坊主でせう。」とつけ加へた。
casual.label: house-checked

casual.en: The monk at Hodoji is a barbarian monk come from the Western Regions. Since he both practises medicine and administers arts of the bedchamber, his fame stands high in this neighbourhood — how Chang San's black cataract suddenly took a turn for the better, for instance, or how Li Si's impotence was healed on the spot — rumours all but miraculous are rife. — Both men had heard these rumours. What business could that barbarian monk now have, to go out of his way to visit Liu? Of course, Liu had no recollection whatever of having sent for him.
casual.ja: 宝幢寺にゐる坊主と云ふのは、西域から来た蛮僧である。これが、医療も加へれば、房術も施すと云ふので、この界隈では、評判が高い。たとへば、張三の黒内障が、忽、快方に向つたとか、李四の病閹が、即座に平癒したとか、殆、奇蹟に近い噂が盛に行はれてゐるのである。――この噂は、二人とも聞いてゐた。その蛮僧が、今、何の用で、わざわざ、劉の所へ出むいて来たのであらう。勿論、劉の方から、迎へにやつた覚えなどは、全然ない。
casual.label: house-checked

casual.en: Let me say in passing that Liu is not by nature a man who welcomes visitors. But when one guest is already present and a new guest arrives, he will generally receive him gladly. For he has a childish vanity that might be described as showing off, before his guest, that he has guests. Moreover this barbarian monk of today is the talk of every quarter of late. By no means a guest to be ashamed of meeting. — Liu's motives in offering to meet him lay roughly here.
casual.ja: 序に云つて置くが、劉は、一体、来客を悦ぶやうな男ではない。が、他に一人、来客がある場合に、新来の客が来たとなると、大抵ならば、快く会つてやる。客の手前、客のあるのを自慢するとでも云つたらよささうな、小供らしい虚栄心を持つてゐるからである。それに、今日の蛮僧は、この頃、どこででも評判になつてゐる。決して、会つて恥しいやうな客ではない。――劉が会はうと云ひ出した動機は、大体こんな所にあつたのである。
casual.label: house-checked

casual.en: "What can be his business?"
casual.ja: 「何の用でせう。」
casual.label: house-checked

casual.en: "Alms-begging, most likely. Asking us to bestow alms, I suppose."
casual.ja: 「まづ、物貰ひですな。信施でもしてくれと云ふのでせう。」
casual.label: house-checked

casual.en: While the two were talking thus, presently, led in by the maidservant, there appeared a misshapen monk of tall stature, with eyes like purple quartz. In a yellow robe, his grown-out curling hair hanging troublesomely over his shoulders, he stood heavily in the middle of the room with his red-handled fly-whisk still in hand. No greeting, not a word.
casual.ja: こんな事を、二人で話してゐる内に、やがて、丫鬟の案内で、はいつて来たのを見ると、背の高い、紫石稜のやうな眼をした、異形な沙門である。黄色い法衣を着て、その肩に、縮れた髪の伸びたのを、うるささうに垂らしてゐる。それが、朱柄の麈尾を持つたまゝ、のつそり室のまん中に立つた。挨拶もしなければ、口もきかない。
casual.label: house-checked

casual.en: Liu hesitated for a while, but as it somehow grew unsettling, he ventured, "Have you some business with us?"
casual.ja: 劉は、しばらく、ためらつてゐたが、その内に、それが何となく、不安になつて来たので「何か御用かな。」と訊いて見た。
casual.label: house-checked

casual.en: Then the barbarian monk said, "You, I take it, are fond of wine."
casual.ja: すると、蛮僧が云つた。「あなたでせうな、酒が好きなのは。」
casual.label: house-checked

casual.en: "Indeed." Liu, the question being so abrupt, answered vaguely, looking toward Sun Sensei as if seeking rescue. Sun Sensei, composed, was laying stones on the board by himself. He showed no disposition to take part.
casual.ja: 「さやう。」劉は、あまり問が唐突なので、曖昧な返事をしながら、救を求めるやうに、孫先生の方を見た。孫先生は、すまして、独りで、盤面に石を下してゐる。まるで、取り合ふ容子はない。
casual.label: house-checked

casual.en: "You suffer from a rare disease. Did you know it?" The barbarian monk said this as if to press the point. Liu, hearing of disease, wore a dubious look, stroking his bamboo wife as he said:
casual.ja: 「あなたは、珍しい病に罹つて御出になる。それを御存知ですかな。」蛮僧は念を押すやうに、かう云つた。劉は、病と聞いたので、けげんな顔をして、竹婦人を撫でながら、
casual.label: house-checked

casual.en: "A disease — you say?"
casual.ja: 「病――ですかな。」
casual.label: house-checked

casual.en: "Just so."
casual.ja: 「さうです。」
casual.label: house-checked

casual.en: "Why, from my childhood —" As Liu would say something, the barbarian monk cut him off,
casual.ja: 「いや、幼少の時から……」劉が何か云はうとすると、蛮僧はそれを遮つて、
casual.label: house-checked

casual.en: "Drink as you will, you never get drunk, do you?"
casual.ja: 「酒を飲まれても、酔ひますまいな。」
casual.label: house-checked

casual.en: "..." Liu stared at his interlocutor and shut his mouth. In fact, drink as this man would, he had never once been drunk.
casual.ja: 「……」劉は、ぢろぢろ、相手の顔を見ながら、口を噤んでしまつた。実際この男は、いくら酒を飲んでも、酔つた事がないのである。
casual.label: house-checked

casual.en: "That is the proof of the disease." The barbarian monk, with a thin smile, went on, "A wine worm lives in your belly. Unless it is removed, this disease will not heal. I, this poor monk, have come to heal your disease."
casual.ja: 「それが、病の証拠ですよ。」蛮僧は、うす笑をしながら、語をついで、「腹中に酒虫がゐる。それを除かないと、この病は癒りません。貧道は、あなたの病を癒しに来たのです。」
casual.label: house-checked

casual.en: "Can it be healed?" Liu uttered, involuntarily, in an uncertain voice. And he was himself ashamed of it.
casual.ja: 「癒りますかな。」劉は思はず覚束なさうな声を出した。さうして、自分でそれを恥ぢた。
casual.label: house-checked

casual.en: "Healed — that is why I came."
casual.ja: 「癒ればこそ、来ましたが。」
casual.label: house-checked

casual.en: Then Sun Sensei, who had till now listened in silence to the exchange, suddenly put in a word.
casual.ja: すると、今まで、黙つて、問答を聞いてゐた孫先生が、急に語を挟んだ。
casual.label: house-checked

casual.en: "Do you employ some medicine?"
casual.ja: 「何か、薬でも御用ひか。」
casual.label: house-checked

casual.en: "No, there is no need to employ medicine or the like." The barbarian monk answered ungraciously.
casual.ja: 「いや、薬なぞは用ひるまでもありません。」蛮僧は不愛想に、かう答へた。
casual.label: house-checked

casual.en: Sun Sensei from the first all but unreasoningly despises the two teachings of Dao and Buddha. Hence he very rarely speaks when thrown together with a Daoist priest or a monk. That he should now suddenly feel moved to speak was wholly because the word wine worm had caught his interest, for the wine-loving Sensei, on hearing it, grew a little uneasy lest a wine worm dwell in his own belly too. Hearing, however, the barbarian monk's reluctant answer, he suddenly felt as if he had been made a fool of, so with a slight frown the Sensei fell again as before to laying out his pieces in silence. And at the same time it struck him inwardly how foolish his host Liu was to meet such an arrogant monk.
casual.ja: 孫先生は、元来、道仏の二教を殆、無理由に軽蔑してゐる。だから、道士とか僧侶とかと一しよになつても、口をきいた事は滅多にない。それが、今ふと口を出す気になつたのは、全く酒虫と云ふ語の興味に動かされたからで、酒の好きな先生は、これを聞くと、自分の腹の中にも、酒虫がゐはしないかと、聊、不安になつて来たのである。所が、蛮僧の不承不承な答を聞くと、急に、自分が莫迦にされたやうな気がしたので、先生はちよいと顔をしかめながら、又元の通り、黙々として棋子を下しはじめた。さうして、それと同時に、内心、こんな横柄な坊主に会つたり何ぞする主人の劉を、莫迦げてゐると思ひ出した。
casual.label: house-checked

casual.en: Liu, for his part, of course paid no heed to any such thing.
casual.ja: 劉の方では、勿論そんな事には頓着しない。
casual.label: house-checked

casual.en: "Then do you use needles?"
casual.ja: 「では、針でも使ひますかな。」
casual.label: house-checked

casual.en: "Nothing so elaborate as that."
casual.ja: 「なに、もつと造作のない事です。」
casual.label: house-checked

casual.en: "Then is it an incantation?"
casual.ja: 「では呪ですかな。」
casual.label: house-checked

casual.en: "No, nor is it an incantation."
casual.ja: 「いや、呪でもありません。」
casual.label: house-checked

casual.en: After repeating such exchanges, the barbarian monk briefly explained his cure to them. — According to it, one need only strip naked and lie still in the sun. To Liu it seemed a very easy matter. If so small a thing would heal him, there was nothing better than to be healed. Moreover, though he was not conscious of it, curiosity was also somewhat stirred at the prospect of undergoing the barbarian monk's treatment.
casual.ja: かう云ふ会話を繰返した末に、蛮僧は、簡単に、その療法を説明して聞かせた。――それによるに、唯、裸になつて、日向にぢつとしてゐさへすればよいと云ふのである。劉には、それが、甚、容易な事のやうに思はれた。その位の事で癒るなら、癒して貰ふのに越した事はない。その上、意識してはゐなかつたが、蛮僧の治療を受けると云ふ点で、好奇心も少しは動いてゐた。
casual.label: house-checked

casual.en: So that at last Liu himself bowed his head and it was agreed: "Then pray heal me, if you will." — Such is the history behind Liu's lying naked on the threshing ground in the blazing sun.
casual.ja: そこでとうとう、劉も、こつちから頭を下げて、「では、どうか一つ、癒して頂きませう。」と云ふ事になつた。――劉が、裸で、炎天の打麦場にねころんでゐるのには、かう云ふ謂れが、あるのである。
casual.label: house-checked

casual.en: The barbarian monk then, saying he must not stir, wound Liu's body round and round with thin cord. Then he bade one of the manservants bring a single wine-filled unglazed jar to Liu's pillow. That Sun Sensei, his boon companion of the wine-mound, should as things fell out stand witness to this strange cure goes without saying.
casual.ja: すると蛮僧は、身動きをしてはいけないと云ふので、劉の体を細引で、ぐるぐる巻にした。それから、僮僕の一人に云ひつけて、酒を入れた素焼の瓶を一つ、劉の枕もとへ持つて来させた。当座の行きがかりで、糟邱の良友たる孫先生が、この不思議な療治に立合ふ事になつたのは云ふまでもない。
casual.label: house-checked

casual.en: What sort of thing a wine worm is, what becomes of one when it is gone from the belly, what the wine jar at the pillow is meant for — none knows these things but the barbarian monk. Put so, Liu, who has gone out naked into the blazing sun knowing nothing, may seem grossly fatuous, but what ordinary men undergo when they receive a school education, for instance, is in truth for the most part doing much the same thing.
casual.ja: 酒虫と云ふ物が、どんな物だか、それが腹の中にゐなくなると、どうなるのだか、枕もとにある酒の瓶は、何にするつもりなのだか、それを知つてゐるのは、蛮僧の外に一人もない。かう云ふと、何も知らずに、炎天へ裸で出てゐる劉は、甚、迂濶なやうに思はれるが、普通の人間が、学校の教育などをうけるのも、実は大抵、これと同じやうな事をしてゐるのである。
casual.label: house-checked

casual.en: III
casual.ja: 三
casual.label: house-checked

casual.en: It is hot. Sweat wells prickling up on his forehead, and when it seems to have beaded it comes trickling lukewarm toward his eyes. As ill luck will have it he is bound with thin cord, so of course he cannot put out a hand to wipe it away. He tries moving his neck to turn the sweat from its path, but at that instant he feels a violent dizziness about to come on, so to his regret he gives up that plan too. Meanwhile the sweat unreservedly wets his eyelids, and circling from the side of his nose round his mouth, runs down under his chin. The nastiness is beyond measure.
casual.ja: 暑い。額へ汗がぢりぢりと湧いて来て、それが玉になつたかと思ふと、つうつと生暖く、眼の方へ流れて来る。生憎、細引でしばられてゐるから、手を出して拭ふ訳には、勿論行かない。そこで、首を動かして、汗の進路を変へやうとすると、その途端に、はげしく眩暈がしさうな気がしたので、残念ながら、この計画も亦、見合せる事にした。その中に、汗は遠慮なく、眶をぬらして、鼻の側から口許をまはりながら、頤の下まで流れて行く。気味が悪い事夥しい。
casual.label: house-checked

casual.en: Until then he had kept his eyes open, gazing hard at the sky scorched white and the hemp-field with its drooping leaves, but once the sweat began to pour without restraint he had to give even that up. It was then that Liu learned for the first time that sweat stings when it gets into the eyes. So, wearing the face of a sheep in the slaughterhouse, meekly shutting his eyes while he lies still beneath the beating sun, he begins by degrees to feel a certain pain in the skin of the upward-facing parts of him, face or body alike. Over the whole surface of the skin a force is at work urging it to move in every direction at once, while the skin itself has not the least elasticity to answer it with; a pain that might best be described as a smarting all over. This is not the misery of mere sweating. Liu began to feel a little bitter at having taken the barbarian monk's cure.
casual.ja: それまでは、眼を開いて、白く焦された空や、葉をたらした麻畑を、まじ〳〵と眺めてゐたが、汗が無暗に流れるやうになつてからは、それさへ断念しなければならなくなつた。劉は、この時、始めて、汗が眼にはいると、しみるものだと云ふ事を、知つたのである。そこで、屠所の羊の様な顔をして、神妙に眼をつぶりながら、ぢつと日に照りつけられてゐると、今度は、顔と云はず体と云はず、上になつてゐる部分の皮膚が、次第に或痛みを感じるやうになつて来た。皮膚の全面に、あらゆる方向へ動かうとする力が働いてゐるが、皮膚自身は、それに対して、毫も弾力を持つてゐない。それでどこもかしこも、ぴり〳〵する――とでも説明したら、よからうと思ふ痛みである。これは、汗所の苦しさではない。劉は、少し蛮僧の治療をうけたのが、忌々しくなつて来た。
casual.label: house-checked

casual.en: Yet this, as he came to think afterward, was still of the less painful order. — Before long his throat grew parched. Liu too knows the tale of how Cao Mengde, or someone, cured his soldiers' thirst by telling them there was a plum grove ahead. But in this present case, however he pictures the sweet-sour plum in his mind, his throat is thirsty just the same as before. He moves his chin, he bites his tongue, but the inside of his mouth still holds its heat. Even that might have been a little easier to bear, had it not been for the unglazed jar at his pillow. For from the mouth of the jar the rich wine-aroma assails his nose without pause. And, perhaps only in fancy, that aroma seems to grow stronger with every minute. Thinking at least to look at the jar, Liu opens his eyes. Straining them upward, he takes in the mouth of the jar and perhaps half of its broadly swollen belly. That is all he takes in with his eyes, but at the same time there rises in his imagination the golden-yellow wine lying brimful and still in the jar's dim interior. Before he knows it he licks his cracked lips round with his dry tongue, but there is no sign of saliva welling. Even his sweat by now is dried by the sun and no longer flows as before.
casual.ja: しかし、これは、後になつて考へて見ると、まだ苦しくない方の部だつたのである。――そのうちに、喉が渇いて来た。劉も、曹孟徳か誰かが、前路に梅林ありと云つて、軍士の渇を医したと云ふ事は知つてゐる。が、今の場合、いくら、梅子の甘酸を念頭に浮べて見ても、喉の渇く事は、少しも前と変りがない。頤を動かして見たり、舌を噛んで見たりしたが、口の中は依然として熱を持つてゐる。それも、枕もとの素焼の瓶がなかつたら、まだ幾分でも、我慢がし易かつたのに違ひない。所が、瓶の口からは、芬々たる酒香が、間断なく、劉の鼻を襲つて来る。しかも、気のせいか、その酒香が、一分毎に、益々高くなつて来るやうな心もちさへする。劉は、せめて、瓶だけでも見ようと思つて、眼をあけた。上眼を使つて見ると、瓶の口と、応揚にふくれた胴の半分ばかりが、眼にはいる。眼にはいるのは、それだけであるが、同時に、劉の想像には、その瓶のうす暗い内部に、黄金のやうな色をした酒のなみ〳〵と湛へてゐる容子が、浮んで来た。思はず、ひびの出来た唇を、乾いた舌で舐めまはして見たが、唾の湧く気色は、更にない。汗さへ今では、日に干されて、前のやうには、流れなくなつてしまつた。
casual.label: house-checked

casual.en: Then violent dizziness comes, two or three times in succession. The headache has been unbroken since a while back. In his heart Liu curses the barbarian monk ever more bitterly. And then he thinks too why a man such as himself should have let such a fellow's patter lead him into this idiotic suffering. Meanwhile his throat grows ever thirstier. His chest turns strangely queasy. He can no longer lie still for endurance. So at last, resolving himself, Liu opens his gasping mouth, meaning to ask the monk at his pillow to call off the cure. —
casual.ja: すると、はげしい眩暈が、つづいて、二三度起つた。頭痛はさつきから、しつきりなしにしてゐる。劉は、心の中で愈、蛮僧を怨めしく思つた。それから又何故、自分ともあるものが、あんな人間の口車に乗つて、こんな莫迦げた苦しみをするのだらうとも思つた。そのうちに、喉は、益々、渇いて来る。胸は妙にむかついて来る。もう我慢にも、ぢつとしてはゐられない。そこで劉はとう〳〵思切つて、枕もとの蛮僧に、療治の中止を申込むつもりで、喘ぎながら、口を開いた。――
casual.label: house-checked

casual.en: But at that very instant. Liu begins to feel an unnameable lump creeping little by little up from his breast toward his throat. At one moment it seems to writhe like an earthworm, at another to edge itself along like a gecko. In any case some soft thing, soft as it is, comes squirming up the gullet. And at last, when it seems to have forced its way beneath his Adam's apple, all at once, slimily, like a loach or something, it slips out of the dark and flies outwards with force.
casual.ja: すると、その途端である。劉は、何とも知れない塊が、少しづゝ胸から喉へ這ひ上つて来るのを感じ出した。それが或は蚯蚓のやうに、蠕動してゐるかと思ふと、或は守宮のやうに、少しづゝ居ざつてゐるやうでもある。兎に角或柔い物が、柔いなりに、むづりむづりと、食道を上へせり上つて来るのである。さうしてとうとうしまひに、それが、喉仏の下を、無理にすりぬけたと思ふと、今度はいきなり、鰌か何かのやうにぬるりと暗い所をぬけ出して、勢よく外へとんで出た。
casual.label: house-checked

casual.en: At that moment, from the quarter of that same unglazed jar, comes a small plop, as of something dropping into wine.
casual.ja: と、その拍子に、例の素焼の瓶の方で、ぽちやりと、何か酒の中へ落ちるやうな音がした。
casual.label: house-checked

casual.en: At this the barbarian monk abruptly lifts the haunches he had settled and begins to undo the thin cord wound about Liu's body. The wine worm is out now, he says, he may rest easy.
casual.ja: すると、蛮僧が、急に落ちつけてゐた尻を持ち上げて、劉の体にかゝつてゐる、細引を解きはじめた。もう、酒虫が出たから、安心しろと云ふのである。
casual.label: house-checked

casual.en: "Is it out?" Liu says this as if groaning, and raising his reeling head, out of curiosity forgets even his thirst and crawls naked to the side of the jar. Seeing it, Sun Sensei too, shading the sun with his white-feather fan, hurries toward the two. When all three peer together into the jar, there is a small thing like a salamander, its flesh the colour of red clay, swimming in the wine. It must be about three sun in length. It has a mouth, it has eyes. Somehow it seems to drink as it swims. Seeing this, Liu suddenly feels sick. ...
casual.ja: 「出ましたかな。」劉は、呻くやうにかう云つて、ふらふらする頭を起しながら、物珍しさの余り、喉の渇いたのも忘れて、裸のまま、瓶の側へ這ひよつた。それと見ると、孫先生も、白羽扇で日をよけながら、急いで、二人の方へやつて来る。さて、三人揃つて瓶の中を覗きこむと、肉の色が朱泥に似た、小さな山椒魚のやうなものが、酒の中を泳いでゐる。長さは、三寸ばかりであらう。口もあれば、眼もある。どうやら、泳ぎながら、酒を飲んでゐるらしい。劉はこれを見ると、急に胸が悪くなつた。……
casual.label: house-checked

notes.body: A sun is a traditional unit of about three centimetres, so about nine centimetres long.

casual.en: IV
casual.ja: 四
casual.label: house-checked

casual.en: The barbarian monk's cure took effect at once. From that day Liu Dacheng quite suddenly could drink no more. Now, he says, he cannot even bear the smell. Yet strangely, his health from that time began to fail little by little. This is the third year since he spat out the wine worm, and no trace remains of the round fat figure of former years. Dull, greasy skin wraps the bones of a stern face, and only a little frost-touched hair remains on his temples; they say there is no telling how many times a year he takes to his bed.
casual.ja: 蛮僧の治療の効は、覿面に現れた。劉大成は、その日から、ぱつたり酒が飲めなくなつたのである。今は、匂を嗅ぐのも、嫌だと云ふ。所が、不思議な事に、劉の健康が、それから、少しづつ、衰へて来た。今年で、酒虫を吐いてから、三年になるが、往年の丸丸と肥つてゐた俤は、何処にもない。色光沢の悪い皮膚が、脂じみたまま、険しい顔の骨を包んで、霜に侵された双髩が、纔に、顳顬の上に、残つてゐるばかり、一年の中に、何度、床につくか、わからない位ださうである。
casual.label: house-checked

casual.en: But it is not his health alone that has declined since then. His fortune too has gone downhill in quick succession, and now most of the three hundred mu of fields around the town have passed into other hands. Liu himself has been forced to take up the hoe with unpractised hands, and drags out his wretched day-to-day life.
casual.ja: しかし、それ以来、衰へたのは、劉の健康ばかりではない。劉の家産も亦とんとん拍子に傾いて、今では、三百畝を以て数へた負郭の田も、多くは人の手に渡つた。劉自身も、余儀なく、馴れない手に鋤を執つて、佗しいその日その日を送つてゐるのである。
casual.label: house-checked

casual.en: Why, since spitting out the wine worm, has Liu's health failed? Why has his fortune declined — once the spitting of the worm and Liu's later ruin are set side by side as cause and effect, these are questions anyone is likely to ask. In fact people of every trade in Chozan have asked it again and again, and answered it themselves in every conceivable way. The three answers given here are in truth no more than the most representative chosen from among them.
casual.ja: 酒虫を吐いて以来、何故、劉の健康が衰へたか。何故、家産が傾いたか――酒虫を吐いたと云ふ事と、劉のその後の零落とを、因果の関係に並べて見る以上、これは、誰にでも起りやすい疑問である。現にこの疑問は、長山に住んでゐる、あらゆる職業の人人によつて繰返され、且、それらの人人の口から、あらゆる種類の答を与へられた。今、ここに挙げる三つの答も、実はその中から、最、代表的なものを選んだのに過ぎない。
casual.label: house-checked

casual.en: First answer. The wine worm was Liu's fortune, and not Liu's sickness. By chancing upon a benighted barbarian monk, he willingly brought about the loss of this heaven-sent fortune.
casual.ja: 第一の答。酒虫は、劉の福であつて、劉の病ではない。偶、暗愚の蛮僧に遇つた為に、好んで、この天与の福を失ふやうな事になつたのである。
casual.label: house-checked

casual.en: Second answer. The wine worm was Liu's sickness, and not Liu's fortune. For to drain a whole jar at a single drinking is quite beyond what an ordinary man can conceive. Had the worm not been removed, Liu would before long have certainly died. Seen in this light, poverty and sickness coming by turns should rather be called happiness for Liu.
casual.ja: 第二の答。酒虫は、劉の病であつて、劉の福ではない。何故と云へば、一飲一甕を尽すなどと云ふ事は、到底、常人の考へられない所だからである。そこで、もし酒虫を除かなかつたなら、劉は必久しからずして、死んだのに相違ない。して見ると、貧病、迭に至るのも、寧劉にとつては、幸福と云ふべきである。
casual.label: house-checked

casual.en: Third answer. The wine worm was neither Liu's sickness nor Liu's fortune. Liu had all his life done nothing but drink. Take wine from Liu's life and nothing would remain. Thus Liu is the wine worm, the wine worm is Liu. Therefore Liu's parting with the wine worm was the same as killing himself. In short, from the day he could drink no more, Liu was Liu and yet not Liu. If Liu himself had already ceased to be, it is entirely natural that the health and fortune of the Liu of former days should be lost.
casual.ja: 第三の答。酒虫は、劉の病でもなければ、劉の福でもない。劉は、昔から酒ばかり飲んでゐた。劉の一生から酒を除けば、後には、何も残らない。して見ると、劉は即酒虫、酒虫は即劉である。だから、劉が酒虫を去つたのは自ら己を殺したのも同前である。つまり、酒が飲めなくなつた日から、劉は劉にして、劉ではない。劉自身が既になくなつてゐたとしたら、昔日の劉の健康なり家産なりが、失はれたのも、至極、当然な話であらう。
casual.label: house-checked

casual.en: Which of these answers best hits the mark, I myself do not know. I have merely, in imitation of the Didacticism of the Chinese novelists, set down such moral judgments in a list at the end of this tale.
casual.ja: これらの答の中で、どれが、最よく、当を得てゐるか、それは自分にもわからない。自分は、唯、支那の小説家の Didacticism に倣つて、かう云ふ道徳的な判断を、この話の最後に、列挙して見たまでゝある。
casual.label: house-checked

casual.en: — April of the Fifth Year —
casual.ja: ――五年四月――
casual.label: house-checked

notes.body: The Fifth Year is the fifth year of the Taishō era: April 1916, when this story was first published.

curious.en: I
curious.ja: 一
curious.label: house-checked

curious.en: It is a heat such as has not been known in recent years. Whichever way you look, the roof-tiles of the mud-plastered houses throw back the sunlight dully, like lead, and even the swallows' nests hung beneath them, at this rate, look to steam their chicks and eggs to death where they lie. Still more, every field that is a field, whether hemp or millet, has bowed its head limply in the earth-steam, and not one thing keeps its green unwilted. The sky seen above those fields, perhaps stricken by the damp heat of these past days, is turbid and clouded near the ground though it is fine, and here and there the cloud-peaks float in drops, mere shapes, like hail parched in a roasting pan. — The tale of the "wine worm" begins with three men who have gone out of their way to come into a threshing ground in the blazing sun, in such weather.
curious.ja: 近年にない暑さである。どこを見ても、泥で固めた家々の屋根瓦が、鉛のやうに鈍く日の光を反射して、その下に懸けてある燕の巣さへ、この塩梅では中にゐる雛や卵を、そのまゝ蒸殺してしまふかと思はれる。まして、畑と云ふ畑は、麻でも黍でも、皆、土いきれにぐつたりと頭をさげて、何一つ、青いなりに、萎れてゐないものはない。その畑の上に見える空も、この頃の温気に中てられたせいか、地上に近い大気は、晴れながら、どんよりと濁つて、その所々に、霰を炮烙で煎つたやうな、形ばかりの雲の峰が、つぶつぶと浮かんでゐる。――「酒虫」の話は、この陽気に、わざ〳〵炎天の打麦場へ出てゐる、三人の男で始まるのである。
curious.label: house-checked

curious.en: Strangely, one of them lies stark naked, face upward on the bare ground. What is more, for some reason his hands and his feet are wound round and round with thin cord. Yet the man himself shows no particular sign of minding it. He is short, fresh-complexioned, somehow giving an impression of dull heaviness, a man fat as a pig. Then a handy unglazed jar stands at this man's pillow, but what may be inside that, too, is not known.
curious.ja: 不思議な事に、その中の一人は、素裸で、仰向けに地面へ寝ころんでゐる。おまけに、どう云ふ訳だか、細引で、手も足もぐる〳〵巻にされてゐる。が格別当人は、それを苦に病んでゐる容子もない。背の低い、血色の好い、どことなく鈍重と云ふ感じを起させる、豚のやうに肥つた男である。それから手ごろな素焼の瓶が一つ、この男の枕もとに置いてあるが、これも中に何がはいつてゐるのだか、わからない。
curious.label: house-checked

curious.en: Another is a monk of strange and ancient visage at first sight, in a yellow robe with a small bronze ring hanging from his ear. His skin is black beyond the common, and to see his hair and beard all curled, he would seem a man come from somewhere west of the Onion Ranges. Until now he has patiently waved a fly-whisk with a red handle, driving from the naked man the horseflies and flies that would settle on him, but as might be expected looking a little tired, he has now come beside that same unglazed jar and squats there with ponderous self-importance, in the posture of a turkey.
curious.ja: もう一人は、黄色い法衣を着て、耳に小さな青銅の環をさげた、一見、象貌の奇古な沙門である。皮膚の色が並はづれて黒い上に、髪や鬚の縮れてゐる所を見ると、どうも葱嶺の西からでも来た人間らしい。これはさつきから根気よく、朱柄の麈尾をふりふり、裸の男にたからうとする虻や蠅を追つてゐたが、流石に少しくたびれたと見えて、今では、例の素焼の瓶の側へ来て、七面鳥のやうな恰好をしながら、勿体らしくしやがんでゐる。
curious.label: house-checked

curious.en: The last one stands far apart from these two, under the eaves of a thatched hut in the corner of the threshing ground. This man grows on the tip of his chin a merely formal beard like a rat's tail, and he is dressed in a soap-black cloth gown long enough to hide his heels, with a tea-brown sash whose knot hangs slovenly down. Judging by the way he now and then uses with care a fan made of white bird feathers, he is most likely a Confucian scholar or something of the sort.
curious.ja: あとの一人は、この二人からずつと離れて、打麦場の隅にある草房の軒下に立つてゐる。この男は、頤の先に、鼠の尻尾のやうな髯を、申訳だけに生やして、踵が隠れる程長い皁布衫に、結目をだらしなく垂らした茶褐帯と云ふ拵へである。白い鳥の羽で製つた団扇を、時々大事さうに使つてゐる容子では、多分、儒者か何かにちがひない。
curious.label: house-checked

curious.en: These three men, all three as if by agreement, hold their tongues. Moreover they scarcely so much as stir, so that you would think they take an extraordinary interest in something about to happen, and for that are all holding their breath.
curious.ja: この三人が三人とも、云ひ合せたやうに、口を噤んでゐる。その上、碌に身動きさへもしない、何か、これから起らうとする事に、非常な興味でも持つてゐて、その為に、皆、息をひそめてゐるのではないかと思はれる。
curious.label: house-checked

curious.en: The sun must be exactly at midday. Perhaps because even the dogs are napping, not a single bark is heard. The hemp and millet hemming the threshing ground gloss their green leaves in the sun and rest hushed and utterly still. And then the sky seen beyond them drifts everywhere oppressively with shimmering haze, so that you suspect even the cloud-peaks are panting in this drought. As far as the eye reaches, nothing seems to breathe but these three men. And those three, again, keep their silence like the clay images enshrined in a Lord Guan temple....
curious.ja: 日は正に、亭午であらう。犬も午睡をしてゐるせいか、吠える声一つ聞えない。打麦場を囲んでゐる麻や黍も、青い葉を日に光らせて、ひつそりかんと静まつてゐる。それから、その末に見える空も、一面に、熱くるしく、炎靄をたゞよはせて、雲の峰さへもこの旱に、肩息をついてゐるのかと、疑はれる。見渡した所、息が通つてゐるらしいのは、この三人の男の外にない。さうして、その三人が又、関帝廟に安置してある、泥塑の像のやうに沈黙を守つてゐる。……
curious.label: house-checked

notes.body: Lord Guan is the deified general Guan Yu, commonly enshrined in village temples; his stern clay images were known for rigid, impassive silence.
notes.span: clay images enshrined in a Lord Guan temple

curious.en: Of course, this is no tale of Japan. — It is an event that happened one summer on the threshing ground of the Liu family at a place called Chozan in China.
curious.ja: 勿論、日本の話ではない。――支那の長山と云ふ所にある劉氏の打麦場で、或年の夏、起つた出来事である。
curious.label: house-checked

curious.en: II
curious.ja: 二
curious.label: house-checked

curious.en: The man lying naked in the blazing sun is the master of this threshing ground, a man surnamed Liu and named Dacheng, one of the foremost rich men of Chozan. This man's pleasure is drink and drink alone; from morning on he is scarcely ever known to part from his cup. And that, as the phrase has it, "whenever he drank alone, he would at once empty a whole jar" — a capacity beyond the common run of men. Though, as I have said before, "his fields by the city wall number three hundred mu, half sown with millet," so there was not the least fear that drink should encumber his estate.
curious.ja: 裸で、炎天に寝ころんでゐるのは、この打麦場の主人で、姓は劉、名は大成と云ふ、長山では、屈指の素封家の一人である。この男の道楽は、酒を飲む一方で、朝から、殆、盃を離したと云ふ事がない。それも、「独酌する毎に輒、一甕を尽す」と云ふのだから、人並をはづれた酒量である。尤も前にも云つたやうに、「負郭の田三百畝、半は黍を種う」と云ふので、飲の為に家産が累はされるやうな惧は、万々ない。
curious.label: house-checked

notes.body: A mu is a traditional Chinese unit of field area; three hundred mu marks Liu as a very large landowner.

curious.en: Why he should be lying naked in the blazing sun has a history of this sort. — That day, as Liu sat together with his fellow-drinker Sun Sensei, Master Sun (the Confucian scholar with the white-feather fan), in a well-aired room, leaning on his bamboo wife and fighting out a match on the board, a maidservant came in to say, "A monk lodging, so he says, at Hodoji or somewhere, has come and insists on seeing you, master — how shall I answer him?"
curious.ja: それが、何故、裸で、炎天に寝ころんでゐるかと云ふと、それには、かう云ふ因縁がある。――その日、劉が、同じ飲仲間の孫先生と一しよに（これが、白羽扇を持つてゐた儒者である。）風通しのいゝ室で、竹婦人に靠れながら、棋局を闘はせてゐると、召使ひの丫鬟が来て、「唯今、宝幢寺とかにゐると云ふ、坊さんが御見えになりまして、是非、御主人に御目にかゝりたいと申しますが、いかゞ致しませう。」と云ふ。
curious.label: house-checked

notes.body: A hollow bolster woven from bamboo, leaned against in summer to keep cool while reclining.

curious.en: "What, Hodoji?" So saying, Liu blinked his small eyes as if dazzled, then, raising his fat body that looked hot already, ordered, "Show him in here." Then, with a glance at Sun Sensei's face, he added, "It must be that monk, I suppose."
curious.ja: 「なに、宝幢寺？」かう云つて、劉は小さな眼を、まぶしさうに、しばたたいたが、やがて、暑さうに肥つた体を起しながら、「では、こゝへ御通し申せ。」と云ひつけた。それから、孫先生の顔をちよいと見て「大方あの坊主でせう。」とつけ加へた。
curious.label: house-checked

curious.en: The monk at Hodoji is a barbarian monk come from the Western Regions. Since he both practises medicine and administers arts of the bedchamber, his fame stands high in this neighbourhood — how Chang San's black cataract suddenly took a turn for the better, for instance, or how Li Si's impotence was healed on the spot — rumours all but miraculous are rife. — Both men had heard these rumours. What business could that barbarian monk now have, to go out of his way to visit Liu? Of course, Liu had no recollection whatever of having sent for him.
curious.ja: 宝幢寺にゐる坊主と云ふのは、西域から来た蛮僧である。これが、医療も加へれば、房術も施すと云ふので、この界隈では、評判が高い。たとへば、張三の黒内障が、忽、快方に向つたとか、李四の病閹が、即座に平癒したとか、殆、奇蹟に近い噂が盛に行はれてゐるのである。――この噂は、二人とも聞いてゐた。その蛮僧が、今、何の用で、わざわざ、劉の所へ出むいて来たのであらう。勿論、劉の方から、迎へにやつた覚えなどは、全然ない。
curious.label: house-checked

curious.en: Let me say in passing that Liu is not by nature a man who welcomes visitors. But when one guest is already present and a new guest arrives, he will generally receive him gladly. For he has a childish vanity that might be described as showing off, before his guest, that he has guests. Moreover this barbarian monk of today is the talk of every quarter of late. By no means a guest to be ashamed of meeting. — Liu's motives in offering to meet him lay roughly here.
curious.ja: 序に云つて置くが、劉は、一体、来客を悦ぶやうな男ではない。が、他に一人、来客がある場合に、新来の客が来たとなると、大抵ならば、快く会つてやる。客の手前、客のあるのを自慢するとでも云つたらよささうな、小供らしい虚栄心を持つてゐるからである。それに、今日の蛮僧は、この頃、どこででも評判になつてゐる。決して、会つて恥しいやうな客ではない。――劉が会はうと云ひ出した動機は、大体こんな所にあつたのである。
curious.label: house-checked

curious.en: "What can be his business?"
curious.ja: 「何の用でせう。」
curious.label: house-checked

curious.en: "Alms-begging, most likely. Asking us to bestow alms, I suppose."
curious.ja: 「まづ、物貰ひですな。信施でもしてくれと云ふのでせう。」
curious.label: house-checked

curious.en: While the two were talking thus, presently, led in by the maidservant, there appeared a misshapen monk of tall stature, with eyes like purple quartz. In a yellow robe, his grown-out curling hair hanging troublesomely over his shoulders, he stood heavily in the middle of the room with his red-handled fly-whisk still in hand. No greeting, not a word.
curious.ja: こんな事を、二人で話してゐる内に、やがて、丫鬟の案内で、はいつて来たのを見ると、背の高い、紫石稜のやうな眼をした、異形な沙門である。黄色い法衣を着て、その肩に、縮れた髪の伸びたのを、うるささうに垂らしてゐる。それが、朱柄の麈尾を持つたまゝ、のつそり室のまん中に立つた。挨拶もしなければ、口もきかない。
curious.label: house-checked

curious.en: Liu hesitated for a while, but as it somehow grew unsettling, he ventured, "Have you some business with us?"
curious.ja: 劉は、しばらく、ためらつてゐたが、その内に、それが何となく、不安になつて来たので「何か御用かな。」と訊いて見た。
curious.label: house-checked

curious.en: Then the barbarian monk said, "You, I take it, are fond of wine."
curious.ja: すると、蛮僧が云つた。「あなたでせうな、酒が好きなのは。」
curious.label: house-checked

curious.en: "Indeed." Liu, the question being so abrupt, answered vaguely, looking toward Sun Sensei as if seeking rescue. Sun Sensei, composed, was laying stones on the board by himself. He showed no disposition to take part.
curious.ja: 「さやう。」劉は、あまり問が唐突なので、曖昧な返事をしながら、救を求めるやうに、孫先生の方を見た。孫先生は、すまして、独りで、盤面に石を下してゐる。まるで、取り合ふ容子はない。
curious.label: house-checked

curious.en: "You suffer from a rare disease. Did you know it?" The barbarian monk said this as if to press the point. Liu, hearing of disease, wore a dubious look, stroking his bamboo wife as he said:
curious.ja: 「あなたは、珍しい病に罹つて御出になる。それを御存知ですかな。」蛮僧は念を押すやうに、かう云つた。劉は、病と聞いたので、けげんな顔をして、竹婦人を撫でながら、
curious.label: house-checked

curious.en: "A disease — you say?"
curious.ja: 「病――ですかな。」
curious.label: house-checked

curious.en: "Just so."
curious.ja: 「さうです。」
curious.label: house-checked

curious.en: "Why, from my childhood —" As Liu would say something, the barbarian monk cut him off,
curious.ja: 「いや、幼少の時から……」劉が何か云はうとすると、蛮僧はそれを遮つて、
curious.label: house-checked

curious.en: "Drink as you will, you never get drunk, do you?"
curious.ja: 「酒を飲まれても、酔ひますまいな。」
curious.label: house-checked

curious.en: "..." Liu stared at his interlocutor and shut his mouth. In fact, drink as this man would, he had never once been drunk.
curious.ja: 「……」劉は、ぢろぢろ、相手の顔を見ながら、口を噤んでしまつた。実際この男は、いくら酒を飲んでも、酔つた事がないのである。
curious.label: house-checked

curious.en: "That is the proof of the disease." The barbarian monk, with a thin smile, went on, "A wine worm lives in your belly. Unless it is removed, this disease will not heal. I, this poor monk, have come to heal your disease."
curious.ja: 「それが、病の証拠ですよ。」蛮僧は、うす笑をしながら、語をついで、「腹中に酒虫がゐる。それを除かないと、この病は癒りません。貧道は、あなたの病を癒しに来たのです。」
curious.label: house-checked

curious.en: "Can it be healed?" Liu uttered, involuntarily, in an uncertain voice. And he was himself ashamed of it.
curious.ja: 「癒りますかな。」劉は思はず覚束なさうな声を出した。さうして、自分でそれを恥ぢた。
curious.label: house-checked

curious.en: "Healed — that is why I came."
curious.ja: 「癒ればこそ、来ましたが。」
curious.label: house-checked

curious.en: Then Sun Sensei, who had till now listened in silence to the exchange, suddenly put in a word.
curious.ja: すると、今まで、黙つて、問答を聞いてゐた孫先生が、急に語を挟んだ。
curious.label: house-checked

curious.en: "Do you employ some medicine?"
curious.ja: 「何か、薬でも御用ひか。」
curious.label: house-checked

curious.en: "No, there is no need to employ medicine or the like." The barbarian monk answered ungraciously.
curious.ja: 「いや、薬なぞは用ひるまでもありません。」蛮僧は不愛想に、かう答へた。
curious.label: house-checked

curious.en: Sun Sensei from the first all but unreasoningly despises the two teachings of Dao and Buddha. Hence he very rarely speaks when thrown together with a Daoist priest or a monk. That he should now suddenly feel moved to speak was wholly because the word wine worm had caught his interest, for the wine-loving Sensei, on hearing it, grew a little uneasy lest a wine worm dwell in his own belly too. Hearing, however, the barbarian monk's reluctant answer, he suddenly felt as if he had been made a fool of, so with a slight frown the Sensei fell again as before to laying out his pieces in silence. And at the same time it struck him inwardly how foolish his host Liu was to meet such an arrogant monk.
curious.ja: 孫先生は、元来、道仏の二教を殆、無理由に軽蔑してゐる。だから、道士とか僧侶とかと一しよになつても、口をきいた事は滅多にない。それが、今ふと口を出す気になつたのは、全く酒虫と云ふ語の興味に動かされたからで、酒の好きな先生は、これを聞くと、自分の腹の中にも、酒虫がゐはしないかと、聊、不安になつて来たのである。所が、蛮僧の不承不承な答を聞くと、急に、自分が莫迦にされたやうな気がしたので、先生はちよいと顔をしかめながら、又元の通り、黙々として棋子を下しはじめた。さうして、それと同時に、内心、こんな横柄な坊主に会つたり何ぞする主人の劉を、莫迦げてゐると思ひ出した。
curious.label: house-checked

curious.en: Liu, for his part, of course paid no heed to any such thing.
curious.ja: 劉の方では、勿論そんな事には頓着しない。
curious.label: house-checked

curious.en: "Then do you use needles?"
curious.ja: 「では、針でも使ひますかな。」
curious.label: house-checked

curious.en: "Nothing so elaborate as that."
curious.ja: 「なに、もつと造作のない事です。」
curious.label: house-checked

curious.en: "Then is it an incantation?"
curious.ja: 「では呪ですかな。」
curious.label: house-checked

curious.en: "No, nor is it an incantation."
curious.ja: 「いや、呪でもありません。」
curious.label: house-checked

curious.en: After repeating such exchanges, the barbarian monk briefly explained his cure to them. — According to it, one need only strip naked and lie still in the sun. To Liu it seemed a very easy matter. If so small a thing would heal him, there was nothing better than to be healed. Moreover, though he was not conscious of it, curiosity was also somewhat stirred at the prospect of undergoing the barbarian monk's treatment.
curious.ja: かう云ふ会話を繰返した末に、蛮僧は、簡単に、その療法を説明して聞かせた。――それによるに、唯、裸になつて、日向にぢつとしてゐさへすればよいと云ふのである。劉には、それが、甚、容易な事のやうに思はれた。その位の事で癒るなら、癒して貰ふのに越した事はない。その上、意識してはゐなかつたが、蛮僧の治療を受けると云ふ点で、好奇心も少しは動いてゐた。
curious.label: house-checked

curious.en: So that at last Liu himself bowed his head and it was agreed: "Then pray heal me, if you will." — Such is the history behind Liu's lying naked on the threshing ground in the blazing sun.
curious.ja: そこでとうとう、劉も、こつちから頭を下げて、「では、どうか一つ、癒して頂きませう。」と云ふ事になつた。――劉が、裸で、炎天の打麦場にねころんでゐるのには、かう云ふ謂れが、あるのである。
curious.label: house-checked

curious.en: The barbarian monk then, saying he must not stir, wound Liu's body round and round with thin cord. Then he bade one of the manservants bring a single wine-filled unglazed jar to Liu's pillow. That Sun Sensei, his boon companion of the wine-mound, should as things fell out stand witness to this strange cure goes without saying.
curious.ja: すると蛮僧は、身動きをしてはいけないと云ふので、劉の体を細引で、ぐるぐる巻にした。それから、僮僕の一人に云ひつけて、酒を入れた素焼の瓶を一つ、劉の枕もとへ持つて来させた。当座の行きがかりで、糟邱の良友たる孫先生が、この不思議な療治に立合ふ事になつたのは云ふまでもない。
curious.label: house-checked

curious.en: What sort of thing a wine worm is, what becomes of one when it is gone from the belly, what the wine jar at the pillow is meant for — none knows these things but the barbarian monk. Put so, Liu, who has gone out naked into the blazing sun knowing nothing, may seem grossly fatuous, but what ordinary men undergo when they receive a school education, for instance, is in truth for the most part doing much the same thing.
